technique: the exit — leaving on an image instead of a statement
lesson:
Today we learn one move: the exit. The exit means the poem ends on a thing you can see instead of a sentence that tells you what to think.

Watch the last full part. The poem could stop at an idea, like "The day's a thing you can carry." Instead it gives you objects: "slab steps underfoot, soil ready for what you'll put in it." Then one short push: "So — up!"

Here is why that works on you. When a poem ends on a statement, your thinking stops there. When it ends on a thing you can see, you keep seeing it after the words quit. The steps and the soil stay in your head. The feeling comes from looking, not from being told.

Try this: write your last line as one object a person could point at. Cut any sentence after it that explains the point.

The second time through, listen for how the poem leaves you looking at the ground before it says "So — up!"

Here is the poem.
poem:
Woodsmoke first, before the eyes are even open—
somebody down the valley beat you to the match,
and the cold comes in through the window with that bite
of apples going soft in the grass, of leaf-rot sweetening.
The stove wants feeding. The floor is honest under bare feet.
Outside, the rounds you haven't split are furred with frost,
and the paths you've cleared lie waiting, plain as a kept word—
the rock to be moved, the slabs to be dug clean and set,
work you can hold in your two hands and see the end of.
There's a kind of grace in that, in ground that stays where you leave it.
The kettle's close to singing. The day's a thing you can carry.

Clear paths and new ground waiting—slab steps underfoot, soil ready for what you'll put in it—

So — up!
